utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Court Deputy, call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody. I'm very sorry to say that Judge Argibay won't be able to be with us this morning. In accordance with Rule 15 bis, the remaining Judges decided to continue the proceedings today. Before we hear the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to raise? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just--

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no transcript, because -- I cannot see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I don't know. Maybe we should wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I heard that we have a back-up in the back room, and they will make the transcript unless we need it right now, and I believe that the court reporter will be here in a minute. Shall we go on or shall we wait?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're prepared to go on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem whatsoever, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just had a little business, as I think the Court is aware. If we could go into private session for just a second, and it doesn't -- we don't need the court reporter for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I was told that our court reporter is missing at this stage, so we are going to hear the witness. At this stage I would like to seek the views of the parties, whether you would like to have the witness or we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think, and I'm sure the Prosecution will probably join me, that it's best to be able to track the testimony as it goes along because sometimes there may be a problem with the translation or -- they've been marvelous. I don't want to give any impression that they, you know -- but -- and also, sometimes where counsel needs to go back to a particular answer in order to be accurate with the witness, and fair, it's very useful to be able to look at and see. So, at least for our point of view, we think we would be disadvantaged at this point. And as you know, I am rather exuberant at times in making my record, so I do need that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's correct. And the -- additionally, we would need to make a record of it anyway, meaning that we -- someone would have to transcribe the tapes, which is a very time-consuming and difficult process and would probably create more work in the long-run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For professional and wholly understandable reasons, Your Honours, I subscribe to the suggestions of both the Prosecution and the Defence of Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are promised to get a court reporter as soon as possible. I hope they are -- they don't think today is a vacation, it's a holiday. We will have a break, and we will resume at quarter to ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I apologise to you for the delay. We had some problems in this courtroom, and to tell the truth, it is the first time for me to come across this kind of problem during my four-year stay at this Tribunal. I hope you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps I jinxed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm ready, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Waespi: [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It will be very short, so you can leave very soon. I just would like to clarify a few issues with you. Now, you told us yesterday that the convoy with the wounded people who came to your checkpoint, Zuti Most, it was the Dutch convoy, I believe you said. And my question is, was it accompanied by Dutch people, by Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. There were soldiers, the vehicles were Dutch, and the personnel was Dutch. And they were transporting Muslim -- the Muslim wounded, severely wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, another point I would like to clarify or just raise with you, you told us that, and I quote you: "The convoy was returned from the Muslim-controlled territory. The Muslims did not want to take their own people in, at least that's what the explanation that the leader of the convoy gave to me." Do you remember that you told us that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I told you, and that is what somebody from the convoy told me, that at the separation line after they had reached Muslim territory, they would not take in them, the representatives of the Muslims at that checkpoint wouldn't take them in because these people were practically dead, so they didn't know what to do with them, and they turned them back. This is what somebody from the convoy told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just put to you what the two Dutch reports are saying about that, and perhaps you have heard this explanation as well. They are saying that the convoy with the wounded never reached Muslim territory, but they were stopped at the border, as you say, by VRS soldiers and officers. And then even beaten, and they had to return the Dutch persons with -- they lost some vehicles -- had to return, and then finally reached your checkpoint. Have you heard this explanation as well, for the return of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it. There was a lady, a Muslim woman, who was with the convoy, on the convoy. She told me that they were returned by the Muslims, turned back by the Muslims, that they didn't want to receive them. I hear this for the first time. I don't know what happened afterwards, but this was told me by a lady from the convoy, what I related to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I paraphrased Prosecution Exhibit 851, that's the Dutch report which we have quoted a couple of times, on page 58 and 59. And you may remember we had some debate whether to be admitted into evidence, it's not. But I just put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivic, let me clarify another aspect in relation to this convoy. You told us yesterday, and I quote you: "And I called the brigade. I called Momir Nikolic. There was no one there to help me. I called the duty officer, and I explained the situation to him." Now, my question to you, was that the duty officer of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Whenever I called, I called the duty officer of the brigade, that was the procedure always. I could not call the commander or immediately call Nikolic or any commander. Always whenever I called the duty officer would reply. And as often as not, he would not even introduce himself. I didn't know who he was. I would just dial that particular number, talk to him, and then I would say: "Please pass Nikolic on to me," or somebody else, as the case was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had a direct line to the Bratunac Brigade, then?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a direct connection with the duty officer in the brigade, just that one line. Or perhaps it was the communications service in the bringing. I'm not quite sure, of course. I usually called the brigade on that number. Perhaps it was the communications system, but anyway, the duty officer of the brigade would always reply, and then I would state my business to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a last issue, is the following: When you talked to the brigade duty officer or operations officer, did you tell them, this person on the other side of the line, that you had these wounded people who were -- needed desperate care? Did you tell that to that person?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I did. Of course I did. And I looked left, right, and centre in order to do something. And it also went -- reached Mladic, but somebody told me that he was asleep, and that they couldn't wake him up. And I couldn't let the convoy pass because I didn't have any orders to that effect. So I was asking for help. But nobody helped me until the next day when Mladic came, when he arrived in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you do remember that the Dutch almost on their knees begged you to allow the wounded to be treated. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I remember that. But I was helpless. As I said yesterday, this convoy leader, as far as I can recall, told me that in the night three had died in the vehicles, and he asked me what he was to do. And I said to him, "I can't do anything. I've done everything in my power, but I cannot take any decisions in my own." For all the goodwill that I had, I had no way to act in any different way. I could not proceed otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were just following orders.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: What else could I do? If I perhaps just kept company to this leader of the convoy, but there was nothing I could actually undertake, something which would be meaningful to my mind. And something which would perhaps also be of bearing on my future. Perhaps they would not only remove me from the post, maybe they would send me to battle or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, Mr. Ivic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just sticking with that point, why didn't you ask for Colonel Blagojevic, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, why didn't you inform him that these wounded were there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, I'm repeating for the umpteenth time, that the commander of the brigade, Mr. Blagojevic, did not have, was in no way involved with the passages via Zuti Most. And I said this, that I never was issued any orders from Commander Blagojevic in connection with these passages via Zuti Most. In fact, I practically hardly knew the man because as far as I can remember, Mr. Blagojevic, a short while -- was appointed commander only a short while prior to the fall of Srebrenica. So that I practically had no dealings, no contact with Mr. Blagojevic, nor did Mr. Blagojevic exert any influence on the passages of the convoys. He is absolutely clean as far as that is concerned. He had no influence on it whatsoever. Nikolic was in charge of this, and I have already spoken about that. If I have not managed to solve this problem, to manage to solve problems with Nikolic, if I couldn't do, that I would call the corps. So also, we had the previous commander, Ognjenovic, who was involved to a certain extent, but Mr. Blagojevic never, not to any extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, it was implied, perhaps unintentionally, but nonetheless it was implied that you were a terrorist, engaged in convoy terrorism, denying the citizens of Srebrenica of necessary food. Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And really, I really was hurt by it and I cannot forgive it. Your Honour, Mr. Judge, I don't know how to address you. This is my very first experience in a courtroom. I believe that you did not have sufficient information about what had happened when you asked me this kind of a question. And I regret it. But if you want to solve a problem, you must know all the details of a problem. You perfectly know, I believe, what terrorism implies. You know when that plane hit the Trade Centre. I really behaved in dignified fashion at Zuti Most, although I did have some reason to act otherwise. I have two sisters and both of them lost their 25-year-old sons, so I had reason to behave in all sorts of fashions. But I helped these people who were going out. I threw them cigarettes. I was even reprimanded for what I was doing. Personally, Mr. Ognjenovic told me, "you cannot man the Zuti Most post because you are too much of a man, you are too good of a man." I was criticised for that, and the Dutch can confirm that. And then all of a sudden you put this question to me, if at least you had any proof. I was really hurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to show you concretely a passage from a report prepared by the Dutch themselves in light of the line of questioning that was posed to you. This is from the NIAD report, chapter 4. We've looked at it before, or portions of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of Madam usher. If we could put it on the ELMO. I apologise to the interpreters for not having copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The number of this document is P851, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This would be -- this, Your Honour, because it's a separate section, a different section, will -- I think perhaps should have a D number of 178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us, and you tried to explain yesterday, and I think you even tried to explain today, about your position at the Zuti Most and how you had no real authority. And for the record, I want to read a portion of this report. I want you to follow along, and then I will ask you some questions. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I wish this report was in Serbian, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not. I apologise. The Dutch haven't got around to translating it in Serbian, and we're quite lucky to have it in English, actually. So, you're going to hear it, and I'll go slowly.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here, and I'm reading from the third paragraph, and I'll continue on: "These upper echelons were hard at work on the matter, Akashi and Ogata (the high commissioner for the refugees), wrote in a joint letter to Karadzic about the poor conditions for the population in Sarajevo, Bihac, Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa. Whole families are crying out for food. We can no longer tolerate the violations and exhaustive negotiated agreements. We refuse to accept lame excuses, false allegations, and suspicions or references to uncontrolled elements to justify interference with the free movement of humanitarian goods and stuff. Also, on 4 June, Janvier and Mladic spoke to each other in Zvornik (see the previous chapter), and this agenda included the supplies to the enclaves. In this, Mladic made a link between the supplies to the enclave and the present blockage of the supplies to the Bosnian Serbs from Serbia. As a gesture of goodwill, Mladic was prepared to permit UNPROFOR to be supplied by road from Yugoslavia (which was already the case for UNHCR transport). It was agreed on 6 June that there would be further contact on the matter. Janvier and Mladic agreed that for the eastern enclaves meetings would be held at established venues regarding the need for food and fuel for the UNPROFOR units and the need for humanitarian aid for the population to be supplied by UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For DutchBat, the further course of events was that UNHCR and MSF, which stands for Medecins Sans Frontieres provided Deputy Battalion Commander Franken with data on their need for food, fuel, and medicine for the population. On June 6, Franken indeed handed over a list of the population's and UNPROFOR's needs to the VRS liaison officer for DutchBat, Major Momir Nikolic. Nikolic received the list without comment. Consultation with him on this occasion led to nothing. He had no authority to take decisions. Ultimately, it was not the local military authority that decided whether convoys were allowed through, but Pale. Nikolic's answer that he had no authority would therefore not have come as a surprise. After all, Nikolic's task was only that of a liaison officer. His duty was to communicate requests from the VRS command to (in this case), DutchBat, and to bring the reply back to his command. Otherwise, it was usually not clear to the local VRS commanders why convoys were or were not allowed through. For instance, the VRS commander of the Yellow Bridge checkpoint to the north of the enclave border, Jovan Ivic, also known as Jovo, said that he only received a telex from his command containing detailed instructions, and what he could and could not allow through his checkpoint. The seriousness of the situation had apparently convinced Pale. On the day after discussions with Nikolic, another UNHCR convoy arrived with ten trucks carrying 72 tonnes of food for the population of the enclave. The VRS authorities had scrapped one truck, the one with teaching materials for the schools. Meanwhile, DutchBat supply problems persisted." Let me stop here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivic, in my reading this portion from the official Dutch report that was conducted by the Dutch government as a result of the events surrounding the fall of Srebrenica, were you able to follow it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I think I was able to follow it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What the Dutch are saying here in their report, does it not correspond with what you told us here, and that is that decisions were being made at the highest level of the VRS, and not at the local level, such as at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is quite correct. I repeat, none of the military authorities of Bratunac could have affected the passage of convoys. The civilian authorities couldn't either. It is the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska that decided upon the passage of convoys. No one from Bratunac could decide about that, civilian or military authorities. This has to do with our town, of course, Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you also said that when -- that you had heard that there had been storage of food or goods after Srebrenica fell. Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I remember it well. I think there are records of that. I don't know whether they were accessible to you, to the effect that when the Dutch Battalion left Srebrenica there were tonnes of food that the military police took from their base. People talked about this, and they also said that there was not a single Muslim house in Srebrenica that they did not find enormous quantities of flour in, believe me. Enormous supplies of flour in every house. That's what people said. As a matter of fact, I even saw some people transporting this flour from Srebrenica to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivic, I just have a few questions. If you could be as direct as possible so I can walk you step by step. Okay? Now, you were also asked whether you were tracking the convoys once they left your checkpoint, whether you knew for a fact that the humanitarian aid had been delivered. Do you recall being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go past your post at the Zuti Most to go into Srebrenica to see whether the humanitarian aid was indeed distributed in a manner in which it was intended?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I had no authority whatsoever to make a single move from the checkpoint where I was into the territory that was under Muslim control. I found that question very strange because this was general knowledge. How could I run that kind of risk? You wouldn't dare move in that direction. They would shoot if they would notice you. So why? When the convoy or a convoy would pass by my checkpoint and move on towards Muslim territory, that's where the Dutch checkpoint was, that's where the territory under Muslim control started as well. From that moment, when the convoy would reach the Dutch, or rather as soon as they'd leave me, I would have nothing to do whatsoever with the convoy. I did not have any authority. I did not have any obligations, and it was not possible to begin with. I had finished my job, and then the other side was waiting for them over there. What happened there is something I did not know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to continue to read the next paragraph from the report itself because it may have something to do with your previous answer. "In the meantime, the ABiH in Srebrenica appeared to be taking good care of itself. In May, the ABiH separated approximately 40 tonnes of goods from UNHCR aid that had reached the enclave from the aid to the population. This implied a considerable risk. If the Bosnian Serbs were to find out the aid to the population could be limited even further. It was also noteworthy that the chief of the defence sector in the enclave, Professor Suljo Hasanovic, reported from the enclave to the defence secretariat of the Ministry of Defence of the Tuzla canton that the ABiH had also received some food from DutchBat. For the same reason, if the Bosnian Serbs were to intercept this message traffic, which was not unlikely, irrespective of whether this message was true, it can give the VRS an additional reason for tightening the thumb screws on DutchBat." Now, have you been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe that's now beyond the scope of cross-examination and certainly beyond the knowledge of this witness. How could he comment on even intercepted traffic between warring parties? I don't think that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond, Mr. Waespi accused the man of being a terrorist, of engaging in --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's simply not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's not true. We used the convoy "terror convoy," but we didn't say or even imply anything beyond that. I hope you can understand that. I did not point out that during your first question to this witness. But it's an unnecessary misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. The question was posed, however, by

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened to the food afterwards? And also, Mr. Waespi made a point that this gentleman was intentionally trying to starve out the people in Srebrenica. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the witness has answered this question many times yesterday and today. I don't think you could ask this witness some questions which he did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm merely trying to confirm his answer to the Prosecution on redirect that once it left, how was he to know that the BiH army was starving its own people by taking the goods, the humanitarian goods themselves and not distributing it the citizens of witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How could this witness know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's the whole point which is exactly what I'm trying to point out, the illogic in the Prosecution's question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe this witness has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question: You were at this checkpoint at Zuti Most. It's a small bridge, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Small one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's on the asphalt road. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a series of questions about land mines. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- as part of your duties, were you to patrol that area beyond the asphalt road to areas or territory where there would be mines? Was that part of your function?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. Next to our checkpoint, on the other side of the asphalt road, right by us, 10 metres away was a trench full of soldiers who were in combat formation, who were holding the lines. So on my left, towards Srebrenica, about 10 metres away from me, there were ten soldiers, a unit of ten soldiers. They controlled everything else as far as combat was concerned, weapons, any kind of operations. I was just there for checking what went into Srebrenica and out of Srebrenica. I did not have any authority, even if a mine had been placed 10 metres away from me. I did not have the authority to touch it or to affect it in any way. That was somebody else's job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, at this stage, are there any documents to tender, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. D173, which is the VRS Main Staff notice of agreement. I believe it's dated 2 April 1995; D174, again another VRS Main Staff notice dated 26 May 1995; D175, another notice dated 30 June 1995; D176, a regular combat report dated 4 July 1995; D176 -- the previous one was 176.1; D176.2, which was the daily combat report, this would have been from the Bratunac Brigade, dated 4 July 1995; D177.1, which is a plan on the realisation of approved project, I believe it's dated 19 May 1995; D177.2, which is the regular combat report dated 21 May 1995; and of course, D178, this portion of the NIAD report which is part 3, chapter 4, section 2, which relates to the humanitarian aid and verifies what the gentleman has testified to, that that was -- he had no control at the brigade level to do anything with the goods, and that this was handled by the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Just two points: The first one relates to Exhibit D176.2/2, and as the Defence rightly pointed out, that's already been admitted under P405. And in relation to the NIAD report, we would suggest, I think it's about two or three pages, that chapter, which includes the footnotes, the sources for what Mr. Karnavas has read out, so I think it assists the Judges to see where that comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I believe that the footnotes are included in the document. When you print it out, they come as endnotes. But they are attached to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What's the relationship between this document and the Prosecution's document which is P851?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can assist, there are two reports basically. One is the Dutch debriefing report of, I believe, October 1995 by a Dutch general, about a hundred pages. That's what you just referred to, Prosecution Exhibit P851, which hasn't been admitted in its entirety yet. And the report Mr. Karnavas is quoting today, that's the Dutch NIAD report, that's the Dutch institute for, I think, war documentation which published a report a couple of years ago, three big volumes. I believe that's what Mr. Karnavas quoted from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's 8.000 pages. I haven't moved for the entire document yet. But there's a possibility. But I'm not suggesting that that's the case. But a little reading material for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Those documents are admitted into evidence. As for Document D176.2, we might have two numbers on that document. At this stage, are there any documents to tender on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about the document P851?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We would suggest to have it admitted. There was some debate last time. I think Mr. Karnavas said, you know, he needed to have a close look at the whole document before he could allow it in. I think we reserve -- you reserved the decision for some time later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just to update, I had promised the Court that we would tell you how many times Mr. Butler cited that in his report so that you could get a little more context with it. Because that's something we did offer into evidence with Butler's stuff. But it was declined at that time. That has been prepared. I haven't, you know, had time to get it to the Court yet. But it has been cited many times by Mr. Butler. And I can provide that very soon. In fact, I will excuse myself with this witness with your indulgence so I can get some of this work done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, did you have a close look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I had a close look at it, Your Honour. And if I could restate my position very briefly, obviously I don't mind portions of the document coming in, for instance, when Mr. Waespi made reference to it, if he had chosen to say, for instance, put it on the ELMO or read a portion of it, and for that portion to come in. Obviously portions that Mr. Butler has made references to, those specific paragraphs, I have no objections to. But for the entire report to come in, then it invites sort of a response from the Defence such as with the NIAD report, do I get to put in all 8.000 pages because I'm using snippets of it? I have no objection. I do think that it would raise somewhat of a concern of everyone if I tried to move in the entire document of 8.000 pages simply because I'm using a chapter or two. Those have been my reservations. Now, I haven't -- we haven't sat with the Prosecution to discuss this matter. I would like to see what the Prosecution has to present as far as what portions of it they really believe are necessary. And again, if they're cited in Butler's report, I think they should be coming in if for no other reason because they are cited. And obviously, the analyst, I choose that word with rather some reservation, included it in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I make a temporary decision at this stage because we could not have a document pending for a long time, and I believe those relevant parts of this report are admitted into evidence, which may be added or reduced in the future in accordance with the proceedings or the citing in some other documents. It is so decided. So this document, P851, is admitted into evidence, the relevant parts of that report. Thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. We wish you a pleasant journey back home. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. It was a pleasure to meet, well, most of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, if I could be excused as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll sit until 11.00. So we still have about 35 minutes to go. Are there any protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible for us to finish this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely. That's why we switched the witnesses, Your Honour, so that this witness could be finished. Of course, we may have a little extra time left over, and I was going to suggest that in light of the fact that the next witness is rather longer that we not start him until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But I have to remind you that we are one witness behind schedule. I wonder whether we could make it up next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I believe that we would be able to. What I was suggesting, Your Honour, and obviously I'm at the Court's control, that if we had a half hour left, for instance, not to begin with the gentleman and wait until Monday. That's what I was merely suggesting only because it would allow us, for instance, to meet with him again. And I think -- I would not wish to break up his testimony, not to mention it would cause him more anxiety than he's under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It is our intention to finish the witness -- the next witness today. And it will be very undesirable to have a witness spend the weekend under the oath during the weekend. So we might stay in the courtroom a little bit longer. So whenever we finish the next witness, we'll break. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That will be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Karnavas. The witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there's no need to be nervous. You can just sort of sit back and relax. Could you please tell us what your name is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubomir Beatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: B-e-a-t-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Beatovic. Where are you from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that where you grew up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your JNA service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what year that was.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: 1960, in Maribor, in the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what sort of training or what functions did you carry out when you were doing your JNA service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I attended a six-month course, and I was trained to be a company orderly, a nurse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now were you mobilised in 1992 when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, could you just describe to us very briefly what your -- what you did. What was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I worked as an engineer in the timber industry within the system of the Sipad company headquartered in Sarajevo, but their office in Bratunac. I was the technical director and manager of the factory for the processing of wood and timber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to focus your attention to July 1995, that period of time. All right? And you need to speak up a little bit, just a little bit, so we can pick up on the record what you're saying. Could you please tell us whether you were a member of the Bratunac Brigade in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what position within the Bratunac Brigade you held.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Initially, I was just a plain soldier on the front line. After that, I worked as a company orderly in the 2nd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade. And after that, for health reasons, because I had the rank of sergeant and had been trained as company orderly, I was appointed desk officer in the Bratunac Brigade at which post I stayed until the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that you were appointed desk officer. What -- could you please -- well first of all, how long -- for how long had you held this position prior to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps for about a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have a commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a commanding officer because according to establishment, I could not be that, because I was not a doctor, and we had a doctor. So he was the one; namely, I did my work with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your commanding officer, your immediate commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the assistant commander, Dragoslav Trisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was the assistant commander for rear services. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you would have been within that sector, that unit of the Bratunac Brigade, the rear services?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please describe to us what your functions were.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my functions were mostly the following: To take care about the manning of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Rather, correction of the interpreter, replenishing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the battalion with medical supplies, with painkillers, with bandages, with stretchers, everything which was required for preventive medical action. And I was also in charge of seeing to the fitness, the health condition of the combatants, to monitor their health status, and if there were any one of them falling sick I would take them to the military doctor in Bratunac. We had a small ward attached to the medical centre with some 10 to 12 beds where mostly soldiers who ran a high fever or similar would be stationed there. I saw to them being properly looked after, cared for, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, aside from the training that you had received when you were in the JNA, did you receive --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- aside from that, did you receive any additional training in order to qualify for this particular position?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Technically speaking, did you fit the qualifications for this position?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was required in order to hold that position, the one that you were holding? What sort of a degree or work experience?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, it was doctors that were envisaged for that particular position. But I held it because -- we did have a doctor, but I was just his assistant. That's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated in your earlier answer that you would look after the health and fitness of the soldiers, check up on their condition.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain how is it if you were not a medical doctor that you could carry out this function?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Because, first of all, it was the obligation of the soldiers to report to me as the first instance if they didn't feel well, and then I would check to see whether that was indeed the case. Then I would take them to the military doctor, who would examine them, prescribe the necessary therapy for them, if any was required. So my job was to actually inspect the soldiers on the front line to see whether they were properly bathed, whether they were clean, whether they maintained personal hygiene, whether they needed any painkillers for their headaches or toothaches or what have you. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of this answer, may I ask whether as part of your functions you would visit the front line, the trenches where the men were, of the various battalions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly would you do when you would pay these visits?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I took with me the necessary quantities of medications, the first bandage, ordinary bandage to dress wounds, if people got wounded. And then mainly painkillers, pills to improve the quality of water, also some powder in order to prevent them from getting lousy, I mean the soldiers in the trenches, for delousing purposes. So it was mostly preventive action on my part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you qualified to dispense this sort of medication, the painkillers, for instance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were ordinary medicines for headaches or toothaches that any normal person knows how to use. And of course, I was also trained in that particular respect during the course. Of course, I could not administer any antibiotics or any injections; that would have been dangerous. That could only be prescribed by the doctor and administered by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your job, were you required to prepare reports or to report?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom would you report?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would report to the assistant commander. And a number of occasions, I also attended meetings of the brigade where I accentuated whatever problems I had encountered in terms of the supplies -- medical supplies, that is, bandages and such. And I compiled monthly reports in that respect and sent them to the corps describing the health condition of the men. But mostly, I prepared these reports with help from the doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you have an office within the brigade command at the Kaolin factory?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, later, I had one. But in the beginning, I had premises, a small office, rather, in the medical centre in Bratunac. It was rather a storehouse where the bandages and the pills were kept, and the basic medical necessities as well. Otherwise, the soldiers would be administered medicines in the medical centre itself with assistance from the medical staff, especially in terms of injections and such treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please describe to us your normal day. How would you carry out your functions, your duties on a normal day, if there was such a thing during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was my obligation in the morning to report at 7.00 to the command. My working day consisted mainly of the following: In the morning, we would usually have coffee, and then we would be assigned specific tasks. Even though I had my usual daily routine programme, I had to go to the medical centre anyway to see whether any sick men had turned up for checkups. I would report to the military doctor there, and I would stay with him for most of the day. After that -- most of the time. After that, I would return to the command for breakfast. And then I would return to the medical centre, and there I spent 90 per cent of the rest of my day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you would be given tasks or specific tasks. Who would assign you these specific tasks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my immediate superior was Dragoslav Trisic, and normally I reported to him every morning. And after having reported to him, I would go there. But he knew where I was, so if he needed me, he would call me at the medical centre. Every seven days or so, I also visited the front lines. I went to see and check out the health condition of the soldiers to see what is it that they needed in that particular respect and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What about those who were on sick leave, who were convalescing as it were. Would you check up on them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would. In fact, those who were -- who lived near, I went to see and check on them in the houses to see whether they were indeed using the therapy prescribed them by the doctor. And those who were not very sick would mainly be treated at home, whereas those who had a high fever and were being given injections, they would be treated in the ward which was attached to the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I want to focus your attention to the period dealing with the events surrounding Srebrenica. And I'm going to give you two dates for reference purposes, the first one being July 6, 1995, an established date as to when the activities regarding Srebrenica commenced, and July 11, 1995, which is the day that Srebrenica fell. So my first question is prior to the events commencing concerning Srebrenica, that is, prior to July 6, 1995, were you, sir, given any particular or special or out-of-the-ordinary instructions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed in any way that battle activities were about to commence and for you to be on the ready?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the health centre where you spent, as you've indicated, some 90 per cent of your time, had received any additional medication or medical supplies in anticipation of casualties that might ensue from some ongoing or about-to-commence battle activities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the day that the activities began, July 6, I'm going to walk you day by day from 6 to the 11 and then onwards. On July 6th, did anything unusual, out of the ordinary, occur as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask, where were you on that particular day? Because I believe you told us on occasion, every seven days or so, you would check up on the men on the front lines. Do you recall where you were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the command of the brigade, at the headquarters of the brigade, and in the medical centre. I didn't feel that there was any need for me to go out in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that it wasn't one of -- that period, at least on the 6th, it wasn't the time for you to be visiting anyone at the front line. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On the 7th, the next day, realising that we're speaking close to ten years later, did anything happen that was unusual?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know of anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the 8th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: The same answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The 9th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, the same answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the day before Srebrenica fell, anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the fall of Srebrenica would have been a rather momentous occasion in light of the ongoing activities for the past three years there. Do you recall that particular day? Does it stick out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, in the morning I was at the medical centre. No one knew what was going on in Srebrenica. No one of the medical staff, that is. Around 9.00, I went to the brigade where I found Dragoslav Trisic sitting in his office. And he told me, he asked me: "Do you know that an operation is underway against Srebrenica?" And I said: "I have no idea. No one is saying anything about it, either in the medical centre or in Bratunac." However, after that, stories, reports started arriving, and it all happened the way it happened. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if somebody, if someone from the Bratunac Brigade had been injured in the front line and had been brought to the medical centre and had been treated by the medical doctor, a real doctor, if I could say that, you know, with no disrespect to you, sir, would you be involved on that particular occasion, or would you leave it up to the doctors, the trained physicians to take care of those seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Normally I would be involved, but also I couldn't do anything without a doctor. I could only assist him in the physical sense, for instance, to transport the wounded or something similar. But on that day, we had no such cases as far as I can remember, at least not until 15 hours. After 15 hours, I went home. I mean, 1500 hours, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your routine? At 1500 hours you would stroll back to your home and rest for the rest of the day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and to sleep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back to July 11th, aside from Major Trisic, the assistant commander for the rear services, your immediate superior informing you about what was happening in Srebrenica, did anything else unusual happen that day that you recollect?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I think that nothing else happened. I don't recall anything else happening. Everything appeared to be normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what about the 12th of July 1995? Do you recall that day? That would have been Petrovdan, St. Peter's Day, the day after the fall of Srebrenica. Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was a normal day more or less. Nothing unusual had been going on in Bratunac. I cannot remember anything specific or interesting in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that have been -- would you have followed your normal or usual routine, that is, going to the brigade command in the morning, having your coffee, maybe getting some instructions, and then going on to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether on that particular day, sir, you ventured into Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that at Potocari on that particular day there was a mass of people, Muslim men, women, children, young, old?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of it on that particular day, and were you ever required or requested, I should say, requested to go to Potocari to see what if anything you could do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall -- I just want to make sure that we have a clear record on this. Do you recall whether you learned that the mass of people -- that you learned on that particular day that the mass of people were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that day, did you see -- on that day, the 12th, that is, did you come into contact with the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come into contact with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I certainly did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we get into July 13, which is the next day, it might be time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you finish the events on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe I did. I believe I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will have our break, and then we will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, let's come to the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beatovic, we left off, we just finished the events of July 12th. So now it's the next day, 13th July 1995. Could you please tell us if you recall that day.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: The 13th of July 1995 was somewhat different in relation to the previous days. As previously, it was my obligation to report to the headquarters in the morning, which I did. Then after I left the office, I dropped in on the duty officer's office. When I opened the door, I saw our commander there, Mr. Blagojevic. He was sitting there, and he, of course, noticed me as I was coming in. He told me, he said to me: "Beatovic, do you have medicines?" And I said: "Yes, I do." I didn't know what particular medicine he wanted. He told me to go to the school. He told me there was a group of people there from Srebrenica, that I was to visit them to take medicaments there and to see what their health condition was, whether there were any wounded or sick people among them. And that is what I did. I went to the medical centre --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I want to go step by step.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall what time in the morning that would have been on 13 July 1995 when you went to the duty officer's office and you found Mr. Blagojevic there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was about 11.00 in the morning. It was in the morning hours, around 11.00 or noon. I cannot recall with precision, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing anyone else in the duty officer's office?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. There were two or three men standing in the office. I cannot recall their names at this point. I believe that they were our men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any officers from the Main Staff or the Drina Corps that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, not on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you were told by Mr. Blagojevic or asked whether you had any medicine and to see whether you could go to the school to check up on those people, what did you do? What was the first thing that you did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: The first thing which I did was to go to the medical centre, and I went up to the store and took some medicines from there, some pills. And I stayed there for a while. And then I went on to the school. I arrived there, and those people were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beatovic, I'm going to ask you kindly to let me walk you through this because I want all the details. Okay? So, could you please tell us what pills did you take with you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly painkillers for headaches, for toothache. Generally speaking, painkillers. That is the only medication that I could administer to them to help them. I wouldn't dare give them anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you store this medicine? Where did you have it when you went -- when you left the health centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I had them in my pocket. This was not a large quantity, just a couple of boxes of pills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You say your pocket. Was it one pocket or more than one pocket? Where were these pockets --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, two pockets, in fact. My two pockets. And as they were camouflage-uniform pockets, I could put a lot of medication in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how long you were at the health centre before you left?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Not more than five or ten minutes most probably. I just went inside, and the people were sitting on the floor there with their heads bowed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beatovic, please listen to the question. I know you're nervous. But let me walk you through this. I'm asking you how long were you at the health centre before you left for the school.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Between five and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the health centre, do you know whether there were any doctors there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to any doctors to let them know that you had this order from Colonel Blagojevic to go visit the school?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us from the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to the health centre, how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I walked, on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from the health centre to the school, how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By foot. Okay. How long would it have taken you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you got to the school, could you please tell us first of all what did you notice on the outside of the school? What and who, if anyone or anything?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: There was nobody outside the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Nobody guarding?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go inside the school?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which school are we speaking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: We're speaking about the school, what is now the school. Once upon a time it used to be Vuk Karadzic School, and now it's called Branko Radicevic School.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us which entrance you went into the school, which side of the building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: The main entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got inside the building, could you please tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: There were guards standing there guarding those people. There were about three of them, policemen, military policemen, and two of them were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we get -- before we go on, I just want to make sure that we have a clear answer. You said there were three of them. You said policemen, military policemen, and two of them were soldiers. So if the exact number of those guarding the people were three, how many of them were civilian police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How many of them were military police, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how did you know that they were military police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: By their insignia, by the kind of uniform they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please describe the uniform that they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform, the whole thing from head to feet. That's what two of the men were wearing. They were coveralls. And one of them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other one, the third one?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: He had the usual kind of camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you recognise these people that were guarding the folks inside the school?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I used to see them quite often. I didn't know their names, though. They were younger people. Therefore, I was not exactly in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where had you seen them before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: In the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that, did you form any conclusions as to where they were from and what unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No. Those three men before from our military police, from the brigade. And those two soldiers were also members of our battalion. Their faces were familiar, but not their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you're saying "those two soldiers." So are you saying that in addition to three military police, there were also two soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it would have been five people in total in the school when you went there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you got there, could you please describe to us, other than those five that you saw, what else did you notice?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing else. I noticed there were prisoners there. They were sitting on the floor, heads down, nothing else. They were silent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us first of all where they were located.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: They were located in a small sports hall and two classrooms, a gym, rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how many approximately you were able to see.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I think about a hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that they were on the floor sitting down, heads bowed down. From that, did you form any conclusion as to at least their state of mind?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: They were in a state of shock. They were frightened actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what did you do in light of the instructions or orders that you had received from your commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I passed by them. I halted. And I asked loudly: "Does anyone have any health problems? Does anyone need help?" I told them they should speak to me so I could help them in whichever way I could. However, there was no reaction from those people. No one spoke. So I stayed for a short while, I went out, and I never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us how you addressed them.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I asked them in a loud voice: "Is there anyone here with health problems? Is there anyone here who has pains? Is there anyone here who is injured? Should I dress anyone's wounds?" Whatever problems they had, I was prepared if anyone was injured to take them back to the health centre so they could be helped. However, no one spoke, and there was nothing else for me to do there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use any negative terms such as calling them Turks or balija or in any other way that would further degrade those people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Because I had been born in Bratunac, and this is not the kind of thing I could ever do. It's not my style in general as a human being. I would never insult anyone because I was never insulted by anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. There was no way I could. They had their heads down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether any of them needed the sort of medical attention or treatment that you were clearly incapable of rendering and that would require the assistance of a physician, a trained physician?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether those guarding the individuals were in any way mistreating, either verbally or physically, those individuals --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to those people that were guarding the Muslims that were in the school? Did you speak to the soldiers or the military police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No. I just greeted them in passing, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform -- did you inquire from them as to why these people were being held in that location?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the commander of the Bratunac Brigade had ordered you to check up and to see whether you could provide any medical assistance, painkillers or what have you, the sort of assistance that you were capable of and had been distributing to soldiers of the Bratunac Brigade, did you make any inquiries from the commander as to why those people were being held at that school?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the commander in any way tell you as to why they were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody inform you that they were being held there so that they could be executed later on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suspect in any way that that was the purpose for keeping them there, so later on they could be executed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that ever cross your mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you left, in light of the order that had been given to you and, in fact, you had carried out, did you then go back to the Bratunac Brigade to report to your commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you write a report of any sort that would at least --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't believe that was necessary. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether you informed your immediate commander, Trisic, so that at least you could justify to him how you had spent that time and the reasons for you visiting that particular school on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that visit to the school, which I believe you indicated you were there for a very short time, five or ten minutes, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me back up. How long were you at the school?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Between five and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From there, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed until 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how long that would have been? If you recollect.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps for an hour, about one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that one-hour period that you were there at the health centre, did you by any chance inform anyone at the health centre, be that person a nurse or a doctor, what you had seen and what you had done?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No. I thought there was no need to cause panic. They were not the ones I was supposed to answer to anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And after that, you said you stayed there until approximately 1500 hours. And then what? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where is your house located, just so we know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Heading out of the town centre, it's at a distance of about five or six hundred metres in the direction of Srebrenica to the right of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your house to where the school is located, are you able, with the naked eye, to see it? Are you able to --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you went home on that particular day, which you have stated would have been approximately 1500 hours, did you go out again, take a walk around the town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't go --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't go out to have coffee or a drink or socialise?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I was busy back home, so I didn't go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, the 14th, do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: It was just an ordinary day, just like the 11th or the 12th. Only the 13th was a bit strenuous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the 14th, did you go to the headquarters as was your habit to go there sometime in the early morning hours?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, at 7.00 in the morning. And I stayed for a while. And then I went back to the health centre. And that's where I spent most of my time, about two-thirds of my time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that particular morning, did you have an opportunity to see Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, do you recall whether you reported either to him or to your immediate superior commander, Mr. Trisic, as to what you had seen and what you had done the day before, the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No one asked anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in walking from the brigade command post to the health centre, as was your habit, would you have gone by the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have been able to see the Vuk Karadzic school during that route, the one that you would normally take from the command post to go to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it from there. But the distance must be about at least 200 metres. But I didn't notice anything there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question, whether you had noticed any buses or trucks or anything unusual happening about the time when you were walking from the brigade command post to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR BEATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the day before, the 13th, do you recall whether you had seen any buses or any trucks that would have been parked in and around Bratunac?
